solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Get ready for a boiled egg? One spills a lot

definitions.text: Get ready for a boiled egg?
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as a phrase: spread butter on strips of bread to dip in the yolk
second meaning: a clumsy person who keeps dropping things

explanation.walkthrough: Strips of buttered bread for dipping into a soft-boiled egg are called fingers or soldiers in Britain, so 'butter fingers' is the breakfast job.
explanation.definitionFit: A clumsy person who drops or spills things is called a butterfingers, as if their hands were greasy.

clue.text: What fiddler performs in pub, drunk — ouch!

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of line, so the letters of the word before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
an exclamation of pain

explanation.surface: A pub fiddler, the worse for drink, plays something that makes the listeners wince.
explanation.definitionFit: An up-bow is a stroke drawn from the tip of the bow towards the heel, a basic movement in violin playing.

clue.text: WG hit out with late boundary?

indicators.note: hitting out is lashing about wildly, so the letters named next are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cricket legend W. G. Grace slogs a late boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: WG is W. G. Grace, the Victorian cricketer, and a boundary is a hit to the edge of the field; but here 'boundary' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A talweg (or thalweg) is the line of a river's deepest channel, often used as the frontier between two states.

clue.text: Like tender runners, trimmed fore and aft, requiring rods for support

indicators.note: trimming at the front and the back cuts off the first and last letters

parts.note: tender young runner beans have no tough strings

explanation.surface: Tender runner beans in the garden need canes to climb.
explanation.walkthrough: Runners are runner beans, which grow up canes, so the 'rods for support' fit the garden picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A tringle is a slender rod, such as a curtain rod, on which something hangs or is supported.

clue.text: Pale green reeds growing wild over small acreage

indicators.note: plants growing wild spread in no order, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
a is the abbreviation for acre

explanation.surface: Pale green reeds spread untended across a little patch of land.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Reseda is a greyish-green colour named after the mignonette plant.

clue.text: Roll up as leave cut by half

indicators.note: cutting something by half removes half its length, here the back half

parts.note: a leave of absence, especially for soldiers

explanation.surface: Someone rolls things up because their holiday has been shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: To furl a sail, flag or umbrella is to roll it up neatly and secure it.

clue.text: Early version of the Good Book buried in capital archives

definitions.text: Early version of the Good Book

indicators.note: something buried lies inside, so the letters are found within the following words

parts.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: An ancient Bible manuscript lies forgotten in a capital city's archives.
explanation.definitionFit: The Itala is the old Latin translation of the Bible that preceded Jerome's Vulgate.

clue.text: Part of psalter to study when retiring and then go off

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
milk turns when it goes off

explanation.surface: Someone reads the psalms at bedtime and then dozes off.
explanation.definitionFit: A nocturn is one of the divisions of the night office of matins, a set of psalms and readings.

clue.text: Like guardsmen parading before evacuation of cantonment

parts.note: ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: evacuating empties a place out, leaving only its outer edges

parts.note: the word emptied of its middle

explanation.surface: Guardsmen march on parade before their barracks are cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: A cantonment is a military camp, which suits the guardsmen picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Guardsmen on parade stand and march bolt upright, which is exactly what erect describes.

clue.text: Justice? By the sound of it something regularly observed

indicators.note: this asks the solver to go by what is heard rather than how it is spelt

parts.note: justice is what is right

explanation.surface: A question about whether justice is something we routinely see done.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite is a ceremony or custom kept up regularly, as in religious observance.

clue.text: Some sort of old weapon king sheathed, not required

indicators.note: a sheathed blade sits inside its sheath, so one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: spare means surplus to needs
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A king puts away a sword he no longer needs.
explanation.walkthrough: The vague definition copies Chambers, which calls a sparke simply 'a weapon of some kind'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparke is an obsolete word for an unspecified weapon, recorded in old texts without its exact form being known.

clue.text: Weed, a grass that's unusual in height

indicators.note: in tells us one piece goes inside the next

parts.note: sum in an old sense is the highest point or culmination

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters come in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A grass of unusual height counts as a weed.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters of 'a grass' sit inside SUM, splitting it after its S. Sum in an old sense means the highest point.
explanation.definitionFit: Sargassum is a genus of brown seaweed, the gulfweed that gives the Sargasso Sea its name.

clue.text: Chill in Scots moor I experienced lacking plenty of clothing

indicators.note: stripped of most of its outer covering, the phrase shows only an inner run of letters

parts.note: the inner letters, with the outer ones stripped off

explanation.surface: Someone recalls the cold they felt on a Scottish moor when they were barely dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Oorie (or ourie) is a Scots adjective meaning chilly, shivering or dreary, so it fits 'chill' used as an adjective.

clue.text: Goblin on earth amid trees changing places among immortals

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so the goblin pieces go inside
changing means altering, so the letters of the trees are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: on here means placed beside, joining one piece directly after the other

parts.note: a nis is a friendly goblin in Scandinavian folklore
E is the abbreviation for earth

explanation.surface: A goblin roams the earth among the trees, rising to join the immortals.
explanation.definitionFit: To eternise someone is to make them eternal or immortal, placing them in lasting fame.

clue.text: Wine (not cha) leading to special ecstasy

indicators.note: not with a word means that word is taken away

parts.note: a dry white Burgundy wine
cha is slang for tea, here just the letters to remove
S is an abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: Wine rather than tea brings someone to a special rapture.
explanation.definitionFit: Bliss is perfect happiness, which is a near synonym of ecstasy.

clue.text: Early instrument? Nasty noise I extracted from it

indicators.note: extracting a thing pulls it out, so that letter is removed from the word after

parts.note: a racket is a loud unpleasant din
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sour remark about an old instrument whose sound was a nasty din.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark hints at the joke that an early instrument made a racket.
explanation.definitionFit: The rackett is a Renaissance double-reed woodwind instrument, nicknamed the sausage bassoon.

clue.text: Bubble from poet recreating wonder with lines

indicators.note: recreating means making afresh, so the letters are formed into something new

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A poet blows a bubble, remaking wonder in lines of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet' in Chambers usually means Spenser, who used this spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowndell is Spenser's spelling of roundel, a small round thing such as a bubble.

clue.text: 150 I nominate on new list

parts.note: CL is 150 in Roman numerals
taken as written
to name someone is to nominate them
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone names 150 candidates for a new list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'List' looks like a roll of names, but it is the definition in its sense of a lean or tilt.
explanation.definitionFit: A clinamen is an inclination or swerve, as a ship's list is a sideways lean.

clue.text: Legendary traitor, dead, bloodied, beneath layer of humus

indicators.note: in a down clue, beneath places the earlier pieces below the next one

parts.note: mor is a layer of acid humus on forest soil
D is the abbreviation for dead
covered in blood, so red

explanation.surface: A legendary traitor lies dead and bloody under the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Mordred is the knight of Arthurian legend who betrayed King Arthur and fought him at Camlann.

clue.text: Old Frenchman: on more than half his land he digs in clay

indicators.note: more than half keeps just over half the word, cutting the rest

parts.note: an inhabitant of ancient Gaul
the French word for land

explanation.surface: An old Frenchman works most of his land, digging into the clay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His land' asks for the French word, since the man is a Frenchman.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaulter is a labourer who digs gault, a heavy clay found in southern England.

clue.text: Struggling along a marine has rounded cape, in mid-Atlantic?

indicators.note: to round something is to go around it, so one piece encloses the other
struggling suggests thrashing about, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
C is the abbreviation for cape

explanation.surface: A marine struggles on, rounding a cape in the middle of the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mid-Atlantic' is not a place here but describes something halfway between Britain and America.
explanation.definitionFit: Mid-Atlantic describes accents or culture blending British and American, which is what Anglo-American means.

clue.text: Praises set working, reverse of careless kept in

indicators.note: the reverse of a word is that word written backwards
kept in means held inside, so one piece sits within the other
working suggests the letters are worked over into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
lax means slack or careless

explanation.surface: A reviewer praises a team set to work, but keeps their slackness under wraps.
explanation.definitionFit: To exalt someone is to praise them highly or glorify them.

clue.text: Scottish ass regurgitated stuff to stop working

parts.note: cud is food brought back up by cattle to chew again
an engine dies when it stops working

explanation.surface: A Scottish donkey brings up its cud and then grinds to a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuddie is the Scots word for a donkey, sometimes also a horse.

clue.text: Working together ultimately jockey often restrained frisky greys

indicators.note: something restrained is held in, so those letters are placed inside
frisky horses jump about playfully, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letters of the words after it

parts.note: the final letter of each word

explanation.surface: A jockey and a pair of lively grey horses work as a team, with the rider often holding them back.
explanation.walkthrough: Greys here are grey horses, fitting the jockey.
explanation.definitionFit: Synergy is cooperation in which the combined effect exceeds the sum of separate efforts.

clue.text: At odds with Anglicanism for the moment?

definitions.note: the answer completes the idiom 'for the nonce'

parts.note: non- is a prefix meaning not, against
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone is, for now, out of step with the Church of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Being non-C of E is to be outside the Anglican church; the question mark flags the playful construction.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'for the nonce' means for the present occasion or for the time being.

clue.text: Pump supplying measure of liquid about right

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: a gill is a quarter of a pint
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A pump dispenses a measured amount of liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pump' looks like the machine, but it is the verb, to question someone hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To pump someone for information and to grill them both mean to interrogate them persistently.

clue.text: What drivers go through, lining up targets without tees

indicators.note: lining up means arranging in a fresh order, so the remaining letters are reordered
without means lacking, so those letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written
tee is the spoken name of the letter T

explanation.surface: Golfers line up their targets without any tees.
explanation.walkthrough: Drivers and tees suggest golf, but the drivers are motorists.
explanation.definitionFit: Motorists shift through the gears of a car as they drive.

clue.text: A jaunt abandoned by king finally, involving a flapper?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: abandoned by means left behind by, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: a lark is a bit of fun or an escapade
the final letter of king

explanation.surface: A king leaves an outing, which seems to involve a lively young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: A flapper suggests a 1920s party girl, but here it is a wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Alar means relating to wings, and a wing is something that flaps.

clue.text: Cracks in the skin

parts.note: read plainly: fissures or chaps in the skin, as on lips or hands
the setter's reading is the same: this is a bare medical definition with no wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: This is Azed's competition word: it is given only a plain definition, and readers send in their own cryptic clues for it, so there is no wordplay to find.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhagades are the medical term for fissures or chaps in the skin, especially around the mouth.

clue.text: Rag offering dances for audience?

indicators.note: for an audience means as heard by listeners, not as spelt

parts.note: a hay or hey is a country dance in which dancers weave around each other

explanation.surface: Students putting on a show of dances for charity rag week.
explanation.walkthrough: A rag in British universities is a charity fundraising event, which the surface leans on; the definition is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To haze someone is to rag them, harassing them with pranks, as in initiation rituals.

clue.text: Bones, 50 found in a ruin restored, adult

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so that piece is placed within
restoring means rebuilding, so the letters are put together anew

parts.note: taken as written
L is 50 in Roman numerals
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: Fifty bones turn up in a ruin being restored, along with an adult skeleton.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulnaria is an anatomical plural meaning bones of the ulna, the forearm bones.

clue.text: Heads for Lord's as many dedicated amateur players train here

indicators.note: heads are the tops, so the first letter of each following word is used

parts.note: the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: Many keen amateur cricketers make for Lord's to practise.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the famous London cricket ground, so 'players' looks like cricketers, but they are actors.
explanation.definitionFit: LAMDA, the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art, is a drama school where actors train.

clue.text: Chap going round clubs for a dark spot (little luminance in club)

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so one piece is wrapped around the other

parts.note: a chap is a man
C is the abbreviation for clubs in cards

explanation.surface: A man walks round the clubs looking for a dim corner.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed words give a second route: L for luminance inside MACE, a club.
explanation.definitionFit: A macle is a dark spot in a mineral, caused by impurities.

clue.text: That lot's those likely to succeed after time

indicators.note: after says the following piece comes second in the word

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
heirs are next in line to succeed

explanation.surface: That group are the ones expected to inherit in due course.
explanation.definitionFit: 'That lot's' is a possessive meaning belonging to them, just as theirs is the possessive pronoun.

clue.text: Need lass, wayward, in get-up showing extreme daring

indicators.note: in says the jumbled letters sit inside the next piece

parts.note: a get-up is an outfit

indicators.note: wayward means straying off course, so the letters stray into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wayward girl in an outrageous outfit shows bold daring.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreadlessness is fearlessness, the quality of fearing nothing, hence extreme daring.
